channel.title: The Pointe at Kirby Gate: Senior Living News
channel.description: Senior housing, senior care and caregiving news from trusted publishers, gathered every day by our team. The summaries are ours; the full stories belong to their publishers.

item.title: Survey: families use AI to build senior living shortlists, but tours and staff still decide
item.description: A U.S. News & World Report survey of 502 U.S. adults who were researching senior living, or had recently moved a relative or themselves into a community, found that about 70% used generative AI tools during the search, most often to compare communities on a shortlist. About half of those able to judge said they had run into wrong AI-generated information, most often about the level of care or amenities a community offers and about availability or wait times. Final decisions still hinged on in-person tours and conversations with staff and residents, and three in four respondents said they would check an independent source before choosing. Why it matters: AI tools can speed up a search, but care levels and availability are worth confirming directly with each community, in person.

item.title: Flu season 2026-2027: what the National Council on Aging says older adults should know
item.description: The National Council on Aging has updated its flu season guide for 2026-2027. NCOA reports that in a September 1 update the CDC kept its earlier seasonal flu vaccine recommendations in place, including a preference for certain enhanced vaccines for people 65 and older. The guide notes that in August 2026 the FDA approved the first mRNA flu vaccine in the U.S. for adults 50 and older. NCOA adds that a flu shot can still be given later in the season, that the vaccine lowers the risk of severe illness even if it does not prevent every case, and when to seek care after getting sick. Why it matters: With flu season starting and family gatherings ahead, it is a good time to talk to your doctor, or a parent's doctor, about which vaccines fit.

item.title: Medicare drug costs in 2027: the yearly out-of-pocket cap rises to $2,400
item.description: Kiplinger outlines what changes for people with Medicare prescription drug coverage next year. The annual limit on what a person pays out of pocket for covered Part D drugs goes up from $2,100 in 2026 to $2,400 in 2027, and the maximum plan deductible rises to $700. The deductible counts toward the cap rather than being added on top of it. Average premiums for standalone drug plans are projected to stay close to this year's level. Open enrollment runs through December 7, so plan choices made now take effect January 1. Why it matters: If a parent takes several costly medications, review their drug plan during open enrollment so the new cap and deductible don't come as a surprise.

item.title: Study: Medicare Advantage enrollees less likely to reach five-star nursing homes after a hospital stay
item.description: A study in Health Affairs looked at more than 1.45 million Medicare beneficiaries discharged from a hospital to a skilled nursing facility in 2022. People in Medicare Advantage plans with narrow provider networks were 22% less likely than those in traditional Medicare to go to a five-star facility, and people in broader networks were 13% less likely. Narrow-network enrollees were also less likely to go to the facility closest to home. The researchers say federal network-adequacy rules should be strengthened. Why it matters: If a parent has a Medicare Advantage plan, its network can shape which rehab options are offered after a hospital stay; a benefits counselor can explain how the plan works.

item.title: HHS plans to expand home- and community-based support for people living with dementia
item.description: Home Health Care News reports that the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services plans to improve access to home- and community-based services for people living with dementia as part of its federal dementia-care priorities. Those priorities also include stronger support for family caregivers, including respite and education, and better coordination of care. The article points to the federal GUIDE model, which already takes a home-based approach to dementia care, as an example of this direction. Why it matters: Families caring for a loved one with dementia at home may see more local support, including respite and caregiver education, as these federal priorities take shape.

item.title: Forecast: new senior living construction to stay modest, led by high-end projects
item.description: Senior Housing News reports on a new forecast from real estate research firm Green Street, which lowered its outlook for new senior living supply and now expects growth of roughly 1% in 2029 and 3% in 2030. Most of the projects moving ahead are aimed at the high end of the market, while elevated construction and borrowing costs keep many middle-market projects from getting built. Developers also generally need an experienced operator in place to secure financing. Why it matters: With little new construction coming, openings in established communities may stay limited, so families benefit from starting their search before a crisis.

item.title: Aging Commission of the Mid-South publishes its 2026-2027 Senior Information Handbook
item.description: The Aging Commission of the Mid-South has posted the 2026-2027 edition of its Senior Information Handbook on the Shelby County government website. The free guide gathers local resources for older adults and their families in one place, from emergency services to tax and trustee information and other benefits for seniors. It also lists the commission's Information and Assistance line and its downtown Memphis office, and a Spanish-language version is listed on the commission's resources page. Why it matters: A single local reference for families sorting out services, benefits and contacts for an aging parent in Shelby County.

item.title: November is National Family Caregivers Month, and this year's theme is "Care Connects Us"
item.description: Caregiver Action Network, which has led National Family Caregivers Month every November since 1997, chose "Care Connects Us" as the 2026 theme. The month-long campaign is aimed at the millions of Americans caring for a parent, spouse or other loved one, with the goal of helping them feel less alone and connecting them with information and support. The organization's site lists resources for caregivers throughout the month. Locally, the Aging Commission of the Mid-South runs a Family Caregiver Program for Shelby County families. Why it matters: A good moment to take stock of the help available to you as a caregiver; in Shelby County, the Aging Commission of the Mid-South's information line is 901-222-4111.

item.title: Blood tests for Alzheimer's-related brain changes draw interest, but are approved only for people with symptoms
item.description: NPR reports that more patients are asking doctors about blood tests that look for changes in the brain linked to Alzheimer's disease. In September, the Food and Drug Administration approved two tests that measure a protein called p-tau217. The experts NPR spoke with stress an important limit: the approved tests are meant for people who already have memory or thinking symptoms, as one part of a doctor's evaluation. They have not been approved for screening people who have no symptoms. Why it matters: If a parent is showing memory changes, a blood test may come up with their doctor; it is not a screening test for everyone, so talk to your doctor about whether it fits.

item.title: Alzheimer's Association launches effort to bring earlier dementia detection into everyday primary care
item.description: The Alzheimer's Association has launched a national Brain Health and Quality Care Initiative to help health systems build brain health, early detection, diagnosis and dementia care into routine medical care, starting in primary care practices. The goal is for more people to have memory concerns checked and diagnosed earlier, closer to home, rather than waiting for a specialist. The effort builds on the Association's guidance for health systems on running dementia care programs. Why it matters: If a parent's memory is changing, the family doctor is a good first stop; earlier diagnosis gives a family more time to plan.

item.title: Study looks at why some brains with Alzheimer's changes stay sharp
item.description: Some people have the telltale brain changes of Alzheimer's disease yet never develop dementia. A study in the journal Cell Stem Cell, reported by Newsweek, examined donated brain tissue and found a group of immature neurons that may be linked to that resilience. The researchers see it as a clue to why thinking stays intact for some people, and as a direction for future research rather than a treatment. Why it matters: Early research, but a hopeful sign; a doctor is the best person to talk with about a parent's memory changes.

item.title: Senate report calls for tighter nursing home oversight; assisted living left to the states
item.description: A new report from Democrats on the Senate Finance Committee calls for closer federal oversight of nursing homes, including more transparency about who owns them and stricter staffing standards. Senior living groups are watching because the push could spread to other parts of long-term care. The assisted living trade group Argentum noted that the report does not recommend new federal requirements for assisted living, which continues to be licensed and inspected by each state. Why it matters: Assisted living rules come from the state, so families comparing communities can ask to see the most recent state inspection report.

item.title: New guide: making holiday visits meaningful for a parent with dementia
item.description: With the holidays coming, our new guide offers simple ways to keep visits calm and meaningful for a parent living with dementia. It covers planning shorter, quieter visits, adapting favorite traditions, choosing gifts that suit the person today, and preparing relatives who have not visited in a while. It also reminds family caregivers to plan support for themselves during a busy season. Why it matters: Small changes to holiday plans can make the season easier for a parent with dementia and for the whole family.

item.title: New guide: 10 signs it may be time for memory care
item.description: Our new guide walks families through ten common signs that a parent living with dementia may need more support than home can safely give, such as wandering, missed medicines, falls, changes in eating and a caregiver who is running on empty. It explains what each sign can look like day to day and suggests gentle next steps, from talking with a doctor to touring memory care communities in the Memphis area. Why it matters: A practical checklist for families who are unsure whether it is time to look at memory care.

item.title: Social Security benefits will rise 3.6% in January 2027
item.description: The Social Security Administration has set a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment for 2027, affecting about 76 million people. Higher Social Security payments begin in January 2027, and increased Supplemental Security Income payments start on December 31, 2026. SSA estimates the average retired worker's monthly benefit will rise by about $75, from $2,095 to $2,170. The adjustment is based on the change in consumer prices measured from the third quarter of 2025 to the third quarter of 2026. Beneficiaries can see their new amount in their my Social Security account in late November, with mailed notices following in December. The 2027 Medicare Part B premium, usually deducted from the same check, will be announced separately by CMS. Why it matters: If a parent's monthly budget for care depends on Social Security, this is the figure to plan with for 2027.

item.title: Scammers are using the 2027 Social Security raise to target older adults, inspector general warns
item.description: Social Security's inspector general warns that scammers are using news of the 3.6% cost-of-living increase to contact beneficiaries. The raise is automatic: nobody needs to register, apply, pay a fee or change their direct deposit to receive it. Scammers posing as Social Security or other agencies may ask for money, personal information or a change of bank account, or send links and software downloads. The inspector general says anyone who suspects a scam should hang up, avoid clicking links, check their own account directly at ssa.gov/myaccount, and report it at ssa.gov/scam or the fraud hotline, 1-800-269-0271. Why it matters: A good reminder to share with a parent this season: the COLA raise never requires a call, fee or account change.

item.title: Senior housing occupancy nears a record high as most major markets pass 90%
item.description: New third-quarter data from NIC MAP shows senior housing occupancy across the largest U.S. markets rose to about 90.4%, close to a record. Assisted living saw the biggest gain of any housing type, climbing to about 89.1%, while independent living reached about 91.7%. More than half of the primary markets NIC tracks are now above 90% full. At the same time, new construction remains near historic lows, so the supply of new apartments is growing very slowly. Why it matters: With communities filling up and little new construction, families who start looking early tend to have more choices.

item.title: Family caregivers' out-of-pocket costs up about 60% in five years, AARP study finds
item.description: New AARP research reported by NPR finds that family caregivers now spend an average of about $11,508 a year of their own money on caregiving, roughly 60% more than five years ago. That amounts to around 31% of a typical caregiver's income, and the share is far higher for lower-income households. The story frames the cost of caregiving as rising even faster than rent or gas, putting pressure on family budgets and retirement savings. Why it matters: Caring for a parent at home has real costs that are easy to underestimate; a benefits counselor can help a family look at the full picture.

item.title: AARP: 12 ways family caregivers can get through their hardest days
item.description: AARP collects a dozen practical strategies for family caregivers on days when patience runs thin. The guide covers handling anger when a loved one falls, wanders or makes a mess, including letting frustration out away from the person rather than in front of them. It also addresses dealing with paperwork and bureaucracy, setting boundaries, and making time for interests that caregivers often give up. The advice draws on caregiving researchers, including a Stanford expert on family caregiver stress. Why it matters: Hard days are a normal part of caring for a parent, and having a few strategies ready can make them easier to get through.

item.title: Guides & Resources: our new library of guides for families
item.description: We have opened Guides & Resources, a library of plain-language guides for families comparing assisted living and memory care in East Memphis, written by the people who answer these questions every day. The first guide, Questions to Ask on an Assisted Living Tour, covers what to ask about care, staffing, daily life, cost and contracts, and what to notice while you are in the building. More guides are on the way. Why it matters: a tour is the one part of this decision you can do in person, and the right questions make it count.
